answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for a Cosmos/DocumentDB account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb (e.g. az cosmosdb create, az cosmosdb show, az cosmosdb keys list). This is part of the main Azure CLI distribution (not a separate extension).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform resource: azurerm_cosmosdb_account (resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example").

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: MongoDB-style URI. Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. TLS port is 10255; schemes mongodb or mongodb+srv are used by drivers but standard Cosmos Mongo URIs commonly use mongodb:// with ssl=true and retryWrites=false and replicaSet=globaldb.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Primary billing model is RU/s (provisioned throughput) or autoscale RU/s; serverless is available in some regions. There is also a newer vCore/dedicated compute offering for MongoDB-compatible workloads in some SKUs, but the classic Cosmos model is RU-based billing.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB-compatible API you use the database user credentials exposed by the account (the account username and the primary/read-only keys) via the MongoDB auth mechanism (username/password in the URI). Classic Cosmos master keys / resource tokens apply for management and some APIs. Entra ID (Azure AD) token-based authentication is not generally available for the MongoDB wire-protocol endpoint — drivers authenticate with the Mongo credentials (username/password / SCRAM mechanisms).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo, motor for async Python) or ODMs built on them (Beanie on motor). There is no separate Mongo-protocol-specific DocumentDB runtime SDK — you should use the official MongoDB driver for your language when targeting the Mongo API of Cosmos DB.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Vector index types available on the cluster in my environment: HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. You create a vector index using the MongoDB createIndex command with a vector index spec on the field. Example (pseudo-command you would run in a Mongo shell / driver): db.messages.createIndex( { embedding: "vector" }, { name: "emb_idx", algorithm: "hnsw", similarity: "cosine", dimensions: 1536, m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } ). (Note: exact option names may vary slightly by server version.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's Mongo API does not expose an Atlas-style Lucene index. For full-text you typically integrate with Azure Cognitive Search (index the collection into Azure Search) or use application-side text processing. Hybrid (text + vector) search is implemented by combining a vector index query against the vector field and a text search (Azure Cognitive Search or in-app text matching) and merging/scoring results in the application.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB-compatible API advertises support for specific MongoDB wire versions (newer accounts support newer versions; my target cluster advertises MongoDB 7.0 compatibility). However, not every MongoDB server feature is implemented: multi-shard/multi-partition ACID transactions are limited (transactions are scoped to a logical partition), some server-side features/commands (server-side JavaScript, certain aggregation stages like $merge/$out across partitions) and some admin commands may not be available or behave differently. Always test advanced features against the target account.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full local emulator for the MongoDB API equivalent to the Cosmos DB emulator for all APIs. For development, run a real MongoDB Docker image (e.g. docker run -p 27017:27017 mongo:7.0) and point your app at mongodb://localhost:27017. For testing against actual Cosmos Mongo behavior you must use a live Cosmos DB account.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change Streams support depends on the account's MongoDB API version; newer Mongo-compatible accounts support change streams but older/legacy accounts may not. If supported, you can use the standard driver change stream APIs. Some accounts may require the 'changeStream' capability or a specific server version to be enabled. (Recommend verifying on the target account.)

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: There is a service-specific MCP server named 'documentdb' which provides data-plane inspection and tools for Cosmos DB / DocumentDB. The general Azure MCP server covers many resource-plane operations, but the documentdb MCP server provides Mongo/Cosmos-specific collection/index inspection and query plan tools.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Originally Microsoft marketed a service called Azure DocumentDB (the JSON/document DB) which later became part of Azure Cosmos DB as the SQL (DocumentDB) API. Azure Cosmos DB is the umbrella service exposing multiple APIs (Core/SQL (DocumentDB), MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table). This Azure DocumentDB is not the same as any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB — it's Microsoft's offering that evolved into Cosmos DB.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is Microsoft’s Cosmos DB engine exposing the MongoDB wire protocol; it is not a stock mongod process. That means you should use standard MongoDB drivers, but expect differences in behavior, limits, indexing and some unsupported commands. Applications must be tested against the target account and account-specific limits (partitioning, RU consumption, transaction scope).

answers.question: What database name will this sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_banking_02 for all collections and operations.

answers.question: Which Python client and ODM will the sample use to implement async Beanie-based ingestion?
answers.answer: Use motor (async MongoDB driver) as the Mongo client and Beanie ODM on top of motor/odmantic patterns (Beanie requires motor + pydantic). Installable via pip: pip install motor beanie pydantic.

answers.question: What field and index will be used for vector search in the messages collection?
answers.answer: Store embeddings in a field named embedding (array of floats). Create a vector index on that field (index name emb_idx) using algorithm HNSW (or IVF/DiskANN if available) with params e.g. dimensions set to the model output size (e.g. 1536), m:16, efConstruction:200. Create it with db.messages.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name:'emb_idx', algorithm:'hnsw', dimensions:1536, m:16, efConstruction:200 }).

answers.question: What aggregation pipeline will the sample use to summarise daily message volume and total value by message type?
answers.answer: An aggregation pipeline grouping by message_type and date (truncating timestamp to day) and summing count and amount. Example pipeline stages: [ { $addFields: { day: { $dateTrunc: { date: '$timestamp', unit: 'day' } } } }, { $group: { _id: { day:'$day', type:'$message_type' }, total_value: { $sum: '$amount' }, count: { $sum: 1 } } }, { $project: { day: '$_id.day', message_type: '$_id.type', total_value:1, count:1, _id:0 } }, { $sort: { day:1, message_type:1 } } ].

answers.question: Which environment variable and connection behavior will the sample use at runtime?
answers.answer: Read the Mongo connection URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable at runtime; do not persist the URI. Example usage in code: uri = os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']; client = motor.motor_asyncio.AsyncIOMotorClient(uri, tls=True). Ensure the URI includes ssl=true (or use tls=True) and the correct port (10255 for Cosmos TLS) if not using SRV.
